disclaimer: Original unvalidated discussion exercise based on public safety guidance; not a recalled or official examination item, clinical protocol or validated scoring instrument. Not for patient care. Confirm current local guidance and supervision arrangements.
title: After a mental health crisis: continuity, safety and practical follow-up
setting: A fictional supervised Australian general practice. The clinician has access to local crisis services but has not yet received complete information about a recent assessment. All people and events are invented; no suicide method is described.
case: A 41-year-old adult books a GP appointment several days after an emergency mental health assessment for suicidal thoughts. They say they feel somewhat better but have missed a follow-up call, have limited phone access and are uncertain who is responsible for their next appointment. A support person is available, but the patient is unsure whether to involve them. Present how you would assess current safety and establish a practical continuity plan.
prompts: How would you ask directly and sensitively about current suicidal thoughts, intent, changes since the crisis and whether the person can remain safe now?
What information would you seek from the patient and recent treating service, with appropriate consent, rather than assuming that an earlier discharge proves current safety?
How would you respond if immediate safety is uncertain or risk has increased, including supervisor support and the local emergency/crisis pathway?
If a non-emergency plan is clinically appropriate, how would you collaborate on support, crisis contacts, access barriers and clear ownership of follow-up?
How would you discuss confidentiality and support-person involvement, check understanding and document the communication and safety arrangements?
reflection_rubric: Makes a fresh assessment of immediate safety and takes new or persistent suicidal thoughts seriously; does not infer safety from improved mood or previous discharge alone.
Uses direct, respectful questions and obtains relevant continuity information without replacing clinical judgement with a score, a promise or an incomplete letter.
Seeks urgent supervisor and crisis/emergency assistance if immediate safety cannot be maintained; does not leave the patient unsupported while help is arranged.

Where a supported non-emergency plan is appropriate, agrees concrete follow-up responsibilities, explores reliable contact options and considers trusted support with consent and applicable confidentiality limits.
Documents assessment, consultation, handover and review arrangements, and recognises that crisis contacts or a written plan do not substitute for emergency care when it is indicated.
source_notes: Extends the previously reviewed Healthdirect principles of direct asking, appropriate immediate help, ongoing professional support and follow-up into an original continuity scenario. Healthdirect is public safety information, not a complete clinical post-discharge guideline; this case requires qualified clinician review and local mental-health protocols.
